title: Chaotic waveform load playbook (personal lab)
content:
Goal: quick, repeatable personal experiment to stress end-to-end serving under a nonstationary arrival process (baseline Poisson + high-frequency chaotic bursts). Want to see p99 behavior, batching dynamics, and prefill/warm-cache interactions when bursts overlay an existing steady qps.

Hypothesis:
- Small, rapid bursts with randomized phase will expose inefficient batching timeouts and cause temporary p99 spikes even when aggregate QPS is within provisioned capacity.
- KV cache priming during bursts should reduce token generation work only if the same prompt prefixes recur; otherwise prefix variance will negate cache benefits.

Environment:
- Cluster: dedicated-devpool-3 (4x A100s, 64GB per GPU reserved), model: redwood-3b-quant-v2 (static kv sizing), runtime: rwinf-1.8.3 (local dev build), batching policy: adaptive (max_batch 64, soft_timeout 6ms), concurrency per GPU: 32.
- Harness: custom Go generator (loadgen-chaos v0.2) + k6 for baseline sanity checks. Generates request timestamps from X(t) = baseline + burst(t) where burst(t) = A(t) * sin(2*pi*f*t + phi(t)), A(t) is low-frequency random walk producing intermittent peak multipliers.
- Workload payloads: 3 prompt families
  - P1: short completions (avg 50 tokens) stable prefix (cacheable)
  - P2: variable instruction prompts (avg 120 tokens) high prefix entropy (uncacheable)
  - P3: streaming chat (avg 200 tokens) — measure tail with streaming disabled for clarity

Run matrix (short):
1) Baseline Poisson 150 qps (mix P1:P2:P3 = 50:75:25) — 30m
2) Chaotic waveform centered at 150 qps, burst peak multiplier x3, f = 0.12Hz (burst every ~8s) — 30m
3) Same as (2) but with cache priming (replay top 20% of P1 prefixes) — 30m
4) Increase adaptive soft_timeout from 6ms -> 12ms under (2) — 20m
5) Fixed batching (max_batch 32, timeout 8ms) under (2) — 20m

Metrics collected (per-second):
- requests/sec (observed), tokens/sec, GPU util (per GPU), mean batch size, batch timeout trigger ratio, queue depth histogram, p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side generate-end), tail-sample traces for p99 > 500ms

Selected raw excerpts (aggregated windows):
- Baseline (30m): obs_qps 148 +/- 6, mean_batch 12.4, p50 28ms, p95 68ms, p99 124ms, GPU utiliz 42%
- Chaotic (30m): obs_qps (avg) 152, bursts peak 460 qps, mean_batch 21.9, p50 35ms, p95 150ms, p99 980ms (multiple spikes), GPU util jump to 85% during peaks
- Chaotic + priming: p99 reduced to 360ms during many burst windows but still spikey when P2 share increased; mean_batch slightly higher (24.1)
- Adaptive timeout 12ms: reduced p99 spike count by ~30% but increased average latency p50 -> 42ms (tradeoff)
- Fixed batching small batch (max 32): worst p99 remained similar to adaptive, but more consistent p95; suggests adaptive allowed occasional large batches that starved small-latency reqs.

Quick notes from traces:
- Many p99 traces show request queued for >120ms waiting for batch formation then additional ~200ms generation due to GPU serialization with oversized batches.
- When burst aligns with cold KV (prefix miss ensemble), generation step dominates; priming helps but only if prefix repetition rate > 30% in window.
- Streaming-disabled runs exaggerate p99 (because streaming spreads token latency); re-run with streaming enabled for production-sim tests.

ASCII micro-chart (p99 over 60s window, sample):
[100,120,110,115,130,450,980,720,150,130,145,160,480,920,180,140,120,110,105,430,780,140,125,115,130,140,400,880,600,170,130,120,115,110,100,420,760,130,120,110,125,135,390,820,190,160,150,140,130,110,100,160,430,790,210,180,160,150,140,120,110,100]
- spike clustering visible every ~8-9 samples matching f used.

Immediate conclusions (personal):
- Chaotic/oscillatory arrival patterns induce large transient p99s even with sufficient mean capacity; small increases in batching timeout reduce p99 spikes but hurt median latency.
- KV priming materially helps for high-repeat prefixes (P1-like flows) but not for high-entropy instruction traffic.
- Adaptive batching may create rare large batches that increase p99 due to queueing; need queue-length aware preemption or weighted latency-aware batch flush.

Next steps / follow-ups:
- Repeat with streaming enabled to capture Token-Emit tail behavior (esp for P3).
- Add a run where we throttle new batch admission when GPU util > 78% (safety valve) to see if it smooths p99.
- Implement a tiny patch to runtime: \"max_wait_per_priority_ms\" so high-priority/latency lanes don't join large batches beyond X ms. Quick A/B.
- Share with Rowan/Ibrahim + schedule 30m sync to decide whether this becomes a formal SLO test.

Notes-to-self: keep this harness deterministic seeds documented next run (seed=20250612-bea). Save full trace bundle to gcs://redwood-dev-temp/bench/chaos-20250612 for deeper analysis.

Open questions (floating):
- Is there value in a burst predictor to preemptively open more parallel shards for short spikes? Cost tradeoff vs occasional overprovision.
- How do multi-tenant noise interactions change the burst effect — simulate with 3 tenant groups overlaying misaligned phases.

End of scratchpad.

-- Bea
